# Ὀγκογράφος (Onkographos)

_Onkographos_ is Ancient Greek for "volume-writer": ὄγκος (volume, bulk) + γράφω (to write, and to draw). It writes about volumes and draws them.

> A tree-shaped encyclopedia of volume rendering and voxel techniques, written by a language model running on one home PC from sources it found and read itself. Every claim cites the source it came from.

_7525 entries · index updated 2026-11-12 22:15 · [open the full index](#index)_

## What this is

The goal is an encyclopedia of **everything related to volume rendering**: drawing data that fills space, such as CT scans, smoke, clouds, signed distance fields, voxel worlds, NeRFs, and Gaussian splats. It covers the mainstream methods, the obscure ones, the data structures behind them, and the engines that use them. The bar for every method article is that **a capable programmer can implement the method from the article alone**, together with the articles above it in the tree. Articles are meant to carry all the key information from their sources, so that they can stand in for the sources themselves.

The encyclopedia is a **tree**. Each entry has one parent, and entries are ordered by mechanism rather than application: a technique sits under the method it modifies, a family article holds only what all of its children share, and each child covers only what it adds or changes. The top of the tree has nine branches, fixed by hand:

1. Volume data and representation (grids, compression, sparse structures, level of detail, neural fields)
2. Producing volume data (voxelization, procedural volumes, acquisition, simulation output)
3. Image-order rendering (rays from the eye: ray casting, ray marching, ray-grid traversal)
4. Object-order rendering (splatting, slicing, projecting volume elements)
5. Surface extraction (volumes to meshes: marching cubes, dual contouring, voxel meshing)
6. Light transport in participating media (scattering, shadows, global illumination)
7. Visualization mapping (transfer functions, classification)
8. Differentiable and inverse volume rendering
9. Systems and applications (engines, tools, and fields of use)

The project is currently **a pilot**. Only one branch is written so far, [Ray-grid traversal](#=Ray-grid_traversal): walking a ray through a voxel grid, from [Amanatides and Woo's Fast Voxel Traversal](#=Amanatides_and_Woo's_Fast_Voxel_Traversal) to octree, sparse-brick, and hierarchical variants. Its articles are being checked and rewritten until they are good enough to scale the same process to the whole tree. The [daily summary](/daily) reports progress per day, newest first and updated hourly: the sources found and fetched, the new information extracted, and the articles written with their check scores. The live pipeline is shown on the [status page](/status).

## How it was made

Everything runs on one desktop PC with an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER and an RTX 3060. The reading and writing are done by local open-weight models through llama.cpp. **Qwen3.6-35B-A3B**, a mixture-of-experts model, does most of the work; **Qwen3.8-27B** is being tested as a writer; and **Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B** measures how close a text is to a topic. The pipeline was designed in collaboration between the author, Elijah Furrer, and Claude, a cloud model, which also wrote this page; the articles are written only by the local models.

The pipeline runs in seven stages, each resumable and running all the time. **Discovery** searches scholarly APIs (OpenAlex, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and Europe PMC), GitHub, Stack Exchange, the Internet Archive and Open Library, YouTube, and the big web search engines, the last through a real, visible browser at a human pace. It follows citations and reference lists in both directions and follows links out of fetched pages, and each topic in the tree gets its own queries. **Fetching** downloads the best available full text (open-access PDFs first, then video transcripts, repository snapshots, and archived copies) and keeps the original file; duplicates are merged by DOI, arXiv id, URL, and content fingerprint. **Triage** scores each document for closeness to its topic, after which a model judges whether it is in scope, what kind of document it is, and how much substance it has.

The model then reads each document in chunks and writes typed **notes** per technique: definitions, steps, formulas, parameters, numbers, data layouts, pitfalls, history, and code. **Each note carries a verbatim quote, and a note whose quote cannot be found in the source is thrown away.** Every technique in the notes is next placed in the **tree**, either under an existing entry, as a new child, or merged with an entry it duplicates; topics that fit nowhere go to a review list for a human.

**Writing** builds each entry from its notes, the source passages around their quotes, its parent's shared principles, and its children's overviews, within a length budget set by how much evidence there is. A second pass reviews the draft: it traces the pseudocode on small cases and removes guesses, placeholders, and uncited filler. Finally, machine **checks** score every article on four measures: the share of sentences that carry a citation; **coverage**, how many of the note items reached the article; **faithfulness**, sampled cited claims checked against the quoted evidence; and **pseudocode tests**, in which the article's own pseudocode is run against a reference implementation on random cases. Articles with problems are rewritten with the problems listed, then checked again.

## How to read an article

Under the title is the entry's place in the tree, each step a link, followed by "Also called" with the other names the sources use; long name lists are cut short, and "Show all" opens them. Below the path is the **quality line** with the article's check scores, colored green for good, amber for middling, and red for poor (hover one for details): **cited** (share of sentences with a citation), **coverage** (share of the facts in the notes that made it into the article), **faithfulness** (sampled citations checked against the quoted source text), and **pseudocode** (the article's code run against an exact reference implementation). Next to them are the version you are reading and the model that wrote it.

Method articles have the sections *Overview*, *How it works*, *Operating characteristics* (cost, memory, and limits), *Background*, and *Sources*. Family articles have *Shared principles* and *Subtopics* in place of the step-by-step part. Very small variants with a single source have no page of their own; they are a `###` entry in their parent's Subtopics. Pseudocode sits in closed "Pseudocode (N lines)" boxes so that it does not take over the page; click one to open it. On a wide screen, a table of contents sits beside the article and marks the section you are reading.

A citation such as `[S3]` points to source 3 in the list at the bottom; hover it to see the source, or click it to jump there. In the list, clicking `[S3]` again opens the source's own page, with its archived original (stored on this machine), the exact text the pipeline read, and every article that cites it. `[G]` marks general knowledge the model added without a source. A source can carry two tags: **abstract only**, when only its abstract or snippets could be read (for example, behind a paywall), and **unofficial**, when it is a blog, forum post, repository, video, wiki, or re-hosted copy rather than a published work. The phrase **"Not given in the sources"** means exactly that, since the writer is told never to guess a missing detail.

**Trust an article the way you would trust a careful student's notes.** The text is machine-written and checked by machines, as described above, not by a human expert. Before relying on a detail, follow its citation, and use the quality line to see how well the article did.

## Fixing what is wrong

To **flag a problem**, select a passage and click **⚑ Flag this** (or use **⚑ Flag** in the quality line for the whole article), pick what is wrong (factually wrong, unclear, missing information, pseudocode bug, or other), and say what it should be. Flags are saved on this machine, in `data/flags.json`. The next repair run rewrites every flagged article with your flags in its prompt, next to the checks' findings. The flag then shows "repaired in vN: check it"; read the new version and **Resolve** the flag, or **Reopen** it if the article is still wrong. All flags of an article are listed at its end under "Reader flags".

Clicking the version in the quality line opens the article's **history**: every version with its scores, any old version in full, and exactly what changed between two versions, with added words in green and removed words in red.

## Using this viewer

**Search** from the box at the top of the sidebar: type and press Enter, or press `/` anywhere to jump to it. Results are ranked with title matches first, and the number before each result is how often the words occur in it. Entries in a result's path that also match are highlighted, and "+N below" counts matching entries under it. The menu next to the search box limits the search to one entry and everything below it. The query syntax is small:

- `"exact phrase"` finds the words together, also across hyphens.
- `-word` leaves out entries containing that word.
- Words of up to three letters match whole words only, so `2` does not match `log2`.

[The index page](#index) shows the whole tree with a one-line description per entry; levels fold with the arrows, Expand all and Collapse all work on the whole tree, and the descriptions can be hidden. In the sidebar tree, click an arrow to fold a level, or **right-click** an entry to open it in a new tab, copy its link or title, or expand or collapse its children, everything below it, or the whole tree (Shift + right-click gives the browser's normal menu). Hovering an entry in the tree, or a link in an article, previews it, and hovering a `[S#]` citation shows its source. The **Recent** tab in the sidebar lists the entries you opened last.

Both trees, the sidebar and the index page, work from the keyboard: ↑ and ↓ move, → unfolds or steps into the children, ← folds or steps out to the parent, Home and End jump to the ends, Enter opens, and Space folds.

**Shift + click** an entry anywhere (sidebar, index, results, or inside an article) to open it in a new tab; this is the quick way to open many entries and switch between them with the browser's tabs. Ctrl + click or middle-click opens it in the background. To link straight to a section, hover its heading and click the link icon, or right-click the heading. The browser's Back and Forward buttons work everywhere, and every page has its own link.

The layout can be adjusted: **«** hides the sidebar and **☰** brings it back, and dragging the sidebar's right edge changes its width (double-clicking the edge resets it). **The gear** opens Colors & fonts, where every color on the page can be changed for the light and the dark theme, and any Google font can be used for the article text and for code by pasting its link or its name. These choices are saved in your browser only.

The pipeline keeps running. When it rewrites the index, the viewer **updates live**, reloading the tree and the open article by itself without losing your place.
